title: Permuting the inputs of self-attention
prompt: The input vectors of a self-attention layer without positional encoding are permuted. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The layer has to be retrained for the new order.
options.explanation: The weights $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ are shared across positions and do not depend on the order, so the same trained layer handles any ordering. The tempting thought comes from recurrent or convolutional layers, where order matters.

options.text: The attention weights take new values that cannot be obtained by rearranging the old ones.
options.explanation: Each attention weight depends only on the pair (query vector, key vector), not on where they sit. Permuting the inputs therefore just permutes the rows and columns of the attention matrix; no new values appear.

options.text: The outputs are the same vectors as before, but permuted in the same way as the inputs.
options.explanation: Without positional information, every output is a function of its own query and of the set of all keys and values, so reordering the inputs reorders the outputs identically. This property is called permutation equivariance.

options.text: Self-attention satisfies $f(s(x)) = f(x)$ for every permutation $s$.
options.explanation: That equation describes permutation invariance (the output does not change at all). Self-attention is equivariant, $f(s(x)) = s(f(x))$: the outputs are permuted along with the inputs, they are not unchanged.

hints: Does the attention weight between two tokens depend on where the tokens are in the sequence?
Distinguish equivariance, $f(s(x)) = s(f(x))$, from invariance, $f(s(x)) = f(x)$.
explanation: Self-attention treats its inputs as a set: query, key and value projections are shared across positions, and each output is a weighted sum over all values with weights computed from content only. Permuting the inputs therefore permutes the outputs in exactly the same way (equivariance), with no retraining and no new attention values. This is why positional encodings must be added if the order of tokens matters.

title: The U-Net border weight map
prompt: The original U-Net weights its cross-entropy loss with the map $w = w_c + w_0 \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(d_1 + d_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The map gives its largest weights to pixels in the middle of large cells.
options.explanation: In the middle of a large cell the distances $d_1$ and $d_2$ are large, so the exponential is close to 0. The largest weights go to thin gaps between touching cells, where both distances are small.

options.text: Far away from any cell the exponential term vanishes, so $w$ is close to $w_c$.
options.explanation: When $d_1 + d_2$ is large compared with $\sigma$, the exponent is very negative and the term tends to 0, leaving only the class-balancing weight $w_c$.

options.text: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the distances to the image border in x and in y.
options.explanation: They are the distances from the pixel to the border of the nearest and the second-nearest cell. The map is about separating touching cells, not about the image border.

options.text: A larger $\sigma$ makes the extra weight fall off faster with the distance from the cells.
options.explanation: $\sigma$ is in the denominator of the exponent, so a larger $\sigma$ makes the Gaussian wider and the weight fall off more slowly. A smaller $\sigma$ gives a faster fall-off.

hints: What happens to $\exp(-x^2)$ when $x$ is large?
Which pixels have both $d_1$ and $d_2$ small?
explanation: The weight map has two parts: $w_c$ balances class frequencies, and the Gaussian-shaped term forces the network to learn the thin separating borders between touching cells. The extra term is large only where the distances to the nearest and second-nearest cell are both small, and it decays with a width controlled by $\sigma$. Elsewhere $w \approx w_c$.

title: Unpatchifying ViT tokens to a dense output
prompt: A ViT with patch size $p = 14$ encodes a $224 \times 224$ image. A dense output of shape $C \times H \times W = 3 \times 224 \times 224$ is produced by unpatchifying: a linear layer is applied to every token and its output is reshaped into a patch. Which statement is correct? The options are written as unevaluated expressions.

options.text: Compared with the token grid, the output is 196 times larger in each spatial dimension.
options.explanation: The token grid is $224/14 = 16$ per side and the output is 224 per side, a factor of 14 per dimension. The number 196 = 14·14 is the factor in the number of pixels (area), not per dimension.

options.text: Each token is reshaped into a patch of shape 14 × 14 × 14 (p × p × p).
options.explanation: A patch covers $p \times p$ pixels in each of the $C = 3$ output channels, so its shape is $3 \times 14 \times 14$. A third spatial dimension $p$ does not exist for 2D images.

options.text: The linear layer maps each token to 14·14·3 values.
options.explanation: Each token must produce one $p \times p$ patch for each of the $C = 3$ channels, so the linear layer outputs $p \cdot p \cdot C = 588$ values that are reshaped to $3 \times 14 \times 14$.

options.text: The encoder produces (224·224)/14 tokens.
options.explanation: The number of tokens is the number of patches, $(224/14)^2 = 224 \cdot 224 / 14^2 = 256$. Dividing the pixel count by $p$ instead of $p^2$ gives a number that is 14 times too large.

hints: How many pixels, counted over all channels, does one patch contain?
The number of patches is the pixel count divided by the area of one patch.
explanation: Patchifying splits the image into $(H/p)(W/p) = 16 \cdot 16 = 256$ non-overlapping patches, one token each. Unpatchifying is the inverse: a linear layer expands every token to $p \cdot p \cdot C$ numbers and these are reshaped into a $C \times p \times p$ patch placed at the position of the token. The upsampling factor per dimension is therefore $p = 14$.

title: Overlap pattern of a strided transposed convolution
prompt: A 1D transposed convolution with `kernel_size=5` and `stride=2` is applied to a long input. Consider output positions far away from the border. Which statement is correct?

options.text: `kernel_size` is divisible by the stride.
options.explanation: 5 is not divisible by 2 (5 = 2·2 + 1). It is exactly this non-divisibility that makes the overlap uneven.

options.text: The number of filter contributions per output position is not constant: it takes the values 2 and 3.
options.explanation: Input $i$ writes to the outputs $2i, \dots, 2i+4$. An output $o$ is covered by every $i$ with $0 \le o - 2i \le 4$: for even $o$ these are $i = o/2 - 2, o/2 - 1, o/2$ (3 contributions), for odd $o$ only two. The counts alternate 3, 2, 3, 2, ...

options.text: This configuration avoids the uneven overlap behind checkerboard artifacts.
options.explanation: Uneven overlap is the cause of checkerboard artifacts, and this configuration has it (2 vs 3 contributions). It would be avoided with a kernel size divisible by the stride, e.g. 4 with stride 2.

options.text: Every such output position receives exactly 2 filter contributions.
options.explanation: Only odd positions receive 2 contributions; even positions receive 3. Exactly 2 everywhere would require a kernel of size 4 with stride 2, i.e. kernel size equal to stride times 2.

hints: Write down which outputs the first few inputs write to: input 0 covers outputs 0-4, input 1 covers outputs 2-6, ...
Compare with a kernel size that is a multiple of the stride.
explanation: In a transposed convolution each input adds a copy of the kernel to the output, shifted by the stride. If the kernel size is not divisible by the stride, the number of copies overlapping at an output position varies periodically (here 3, 2, 3, 2), which creates a regular checkerboard pattern. If the kernel size is a multiple of the stride (e.g. 4 and 2), every position gets the same number of contributions.

title: Shapes in a general attention layer
prompt: A general attention layer receives 5 query vectors of dimension 64 and 4 input vectors of dimension 256. The queries are given as an input, so the layer has no query matrix $W_Q$. The key matrix $W_K$ is $256 \times 64$ and the value matrix $W_V$ is $256 \times 128$. Assume vectors are stored as rows, so $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 64}$ and the inputs form $X \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 256}$, with $K = X W_K$, $V = X W_V$, $E = Q K^\top$ and $Y = \text{softmax}(E)\, V$. Which statement about the shapes inside the layer is correct?

options.text: The value vectors $V$ have shape $128 \times 4$.
options.explanation: With vectors as rows, $V = X W_V$ has shape $(4 \times 256)(256 \times 128) = 4 \times 128$: one 128-dimensional value per input vector. $128 \times 4$ would be the transposed (column-vector) convention.

options.text: The key vectors $K$ have shape $4 \times 256$.
options.explanation: $256$ is the input dimension, which is projected away: $K = X W_K$ has shape $(4 \times 256)(256 \times 64) = 4 \times 64$. The key dimension must match the query dimension 64.

options.text: The similarity matrix $E$ has shape $4 \times 5$.
options.explanation: $E = Q K^\top$ has shape $(5 \times 64)(64 \times 4) = 5 \times 4$: one row per query, one column per key. $4 \times 5$ mixes up the roles of queries and keys.

options.text: The output $Y$ has shape $5 \times 128$.
options.explanation: $\text{softmax}(E)$ is $5 \times 4$ and $V$ is $4 \times 128$, so $Y$ is $5 \times 128$: one output vector, of the value dimension, per query.

hints: Write the shape of every product step by step, starting with $K$ and $V$.
The number of outputs equals the number of queries, and their dimension equals the value dimension.
explanation: Shapes: $K = X W_K$ is $4 \times 64$, $V = X W_V$ is $4 \times 128$, $E = Q K^\top$ is $(5 \times 64)(64 \times 4) = 5 \times 4$, and $Y = \text{softmax}(E) V$ is $(5 \times 4)(4 \times 128) = 5 \times 128$. The inner dimensions must match in every product: the key dimension must equal the query dimension, and the number of keys must equal the number of values. The output has one row per query.

title: Nested and full-scale skip connections
prompt: Which statement about nested dense skips (UNet++) and full-scale skips (UNet 3+) is correct?

options.text: UNet++ places convolution nodes on the skip pathways.
options.explanation: UNet++ replaces the plain skip connection by a nested grid of convolutional nodes $X^{i,j}$, so the encoder features are refined step by step before they reach the decoder.

options.text: In UNet++, the semantic gap is widened, because the skips bypass more layers.
options.explanation: The purpose of the dense convolution nodes is to narrow the semantic gap between encoder and decoder features. The skip passes through intermediate nodes instead of connecting directly, which makes the features more similar before fusion.

options.text: In UNet 3+, higher-resolution encoder features are upsampled before they are concatenated.
options.explanation: Higher-resolution features are larger than the target scale, so they must be downsampled (e.g. by max pooling). It is the lower-resolution (deeper) features that are upsampled before concatenation.

options.text: In UNet++, node $X^{i,j}$ receives only the node directly below it.
options.explanation: Node $X^{i,j}$ receives all previous nodes on the same level, $X^{i,0}, \dots, X^{i,j-1}$ (dense connections), plus the upsampled node $X^{i+1,j-1}$ from the level below.

hints: Which direction does a feature map have to be resized to match a different scale?
What is the purpose of adding nodes on the skip path?
explanation: UNet++ turns each skip into a dense, nested grid of convolutional nodes, which reduces the semantic gap between encoder and decoder features. UNet 3+ instead connects every decoder stage to features of all scales: finer ones are max-pooled down, coarser ones are upsampled, and everything is concatenated at the target resolution.

title: Parameters of multihead self-attention
prompt: A multihead self-attention layer has width $D$ and $H$ heads with head dimension $D_h = D / H$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: $H$ heads of width $D/H$ hold the same $4D^2$ parameters as a single head of full width.
options.explanation: Each head has $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ of shape $D \times D_h$, giving $3 H D D_h = 3D^2$ parameters, plus one output matrix $W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ with $D^2$. The total is $4D^2$, exactly as for one head of width $D$ (ignoring biases).

options.text: Each head has its own output projection matrix $W_O$.
options.explanation: The head outputs are concatenated into a vector of size $H D_h = D$ and projected by one shared $W_O$. Per-head output matrices are not part of the standard design.

options.text: The output projection matrix $W_O$ has shape $D_h \times D_h$.
options.explanation: $W_O$ acts on the concatenation of all heads, which has dimension $H D_h = D$, and maps back to width $D$, so it is $D \times D$.

options.text: Each head has its own $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$, each of shape $D \times D$.
options.explanation: Each head has its own projections, but they map to the head dimension, so they are $D \times D_h$. If every head used $D \times D$ matrices the layer would have $H$ times more parameters.

hints: Count the parameters of all query, key and value matrices over all heads.
The heads are concatenated before the final projection.
explanation: Splitting the width into $H$ heads of size $D_h = D/H$ does not change the number of parameters: $3 \cdot H \cdot D \cdot D_h = 3D^2$ for the Q, K and V projections plus $D^2$ for the shared output matrix, i.e. $4D^2$. Multiple heads therefore let the layer attend to several things in parallel at the same cost as one wide head.

title: Losses and metrics for segmentation
prompt: Which statements about losses and metrics for segmentation are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A small epsilon of about 1e-5 avoids 0/0 for classes that are absent.
options.explanation: For a class that is absent from both prediction and target, the Dice or IoU numerator and denominator are both 0. Adding a small epsilon to both makes the ratio well defined (and equal to 1).

options.text: mIoU is the IoU averaged over the pixels of one class.
options.explanation: mIoU is the IoU averaged over the classes. The IoU of one class is already computed over all pixels (intersection over union of the predicted and the true region).

options.text: The target $Y$ is one-hot and has the same shape $K \times H \times W$ as the prediction $P$.
options.explanation: For a soft Dice loss the target is one-hot encoded with one channel per class, so it can be multiplied element-wise with the predicted probabilities $P \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H \times W}$.

options.text: The Dice loss is more sensitive to class imbalance than cross-entropy.
options.explanation: The reverse holds: Dice is computed per class as a ratio, so a small class counts as much as a large one, which makes it less sensitive to class imbalance. Plain pixel-wise cross-entropy is dominated by large classes.

options.text: nnU-Net trains with the Dice loss only.
options.explanation: nnU-Net uses the sum of Dice loss and cross-entropy loss. Cross-entropy provides stable gradients, Dice handles class imbalance.

hints: Is the mean in mIoU taken over pixels or over something else?
Dice measures overlap per class. Which loss is dominated by the largest class?
explanation: Segmentation metrics and losses are computed per class on masks of the same shape as the prediction (one-hot targets), then averaged over classes. An epsilon prevents 0/0 when a class is absent. Dice and IoU are less affected by class imbalance than pixel-wise cross-entropy, which is why strong pipelines such as nnU-Net combine Dice and cross-entropy.

title: Tracing one pixel through PixelShuffle
prompt: `torch.nn.PixelShuffle(2)` turns $X$ of shape $4 \times 3 \times 3$ into $Y$ of shape $1 \times 6 \times 6$, with $Y[0, 2h+i, 2w+j] = X[2i+j, h, w]$ and all indices starting at 0. Which statement about the output pixel $Y[0, 3, 1]$ is correct?

options.text: Its value is copied from the spatial position $(h, w) = (1, 1)$ of the input.
options.explanation: From $2w + j = 1$ with $j \in \{0, 1\}$ we get $w = 0$, $j = 1$, not $w = 1$. The column of the source is 0.

options.text: Its value is copied from the spatial position $(h, w) = (0, 1)$ of the input.
options.explanation: From $2h + i = 3$ we get $h = 1$, $i = 1$, so the row is 1, and $2w + j = 1$ gives $w = 0$. The source position is $(1, 0)$; the row and column indices of this option are swapped.

options.text: Its value is interpolated from neighbouring input pixels.
options.explanation: PixelShuffle is a pure rearrangement: every output value is an exact copy of one input value, with no averaging or interpolation.

options.text: Its value is copied from input channel 3.
options.explanation: Solving $2h + i = 3$ gives $h = 1$, $i = 1$ and $2w + j = 1$ gives $w = 0$, $j = 1$. The channel is $2i + j = 2 + 1 = 3$ (and the position is $(1, 0)$).

hints: Write the output coordinates as $2h + i$ and $2w + j$ with $i, j \in \{0, 1\}$ and solve for $h, i, w, j$.
Then compute the channel with $2i + j$.
explanation: The output coordinate splits uniquely into a coarse part and a sub-pixel offset: row $3 = 2 \cdot 1 + 1$ gives $(h, i) = (1, 1)$ and column $1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1$ gives $(w, j) = (0, 1)$. The source is channel $2i + j = 3$ at position $(h, w) = (1, 0)$. PixelShuffle only moves values from channels into space, which is why a convolution before it learns the sub-pixel details.

title: Fixed sinusoidal versus learned positional encoding
prompt: Which statements about the fixed sinusoidal encoding of Vaswani et al. and about a learned positional encoding are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A learned encoding performs much worse in practice than the fixed one.
options.explanation: Vaswani et al. found nearly identical results for the learned and the fixed encoding. The fixed one was kept mainly because it can extrapolate to longer sequences, not because it is much better.

options.text: The fixed encoding is defined for any position $i$, so it extends to sequences longer than those seen in training.
options.explanation: The encoding is a closed-form function of the position $i$, so it can be evaluated for any $i$. A learned table only has entries for positions up to $N_{max}$.

options.text: In the fixed encoding, each pair of dimensions oscillates at its own wavelength, from $2\pi$ up to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.
options.explanation: Pair $k$ uses the wavelength $2\pi \cdot 10000^{2k/D}$, a geometric progression from $2\pi$ (fast) to about $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ (slow), so the pairs encode position at many scales.

options.text: The fixed encoding is $P(i, 2k) = \sin\left(i \cdot 10000^{2k/D}\right)$ and $P(i, 2k+1) = \cos\left(i \cdot 10000^{2k/D}\right)$.
options.explanation: The position is divided by the factor, not multiplied: $P(i, 2k) = \sin\left(i / 10000^{2k/D}\right)$. With multiplication the frequencies would grow instead of spanning wavelengths from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.

options.text: The fixed sinusoidal encoding has $N_{max} \times D$ trainable parameters.
options.explanation: The fixed encoding has no trainable parameters at all. The count $N_{max} \times D$ belongs to a learned encoding, which stores one trainable vector per position.

hints: Which of the two encodings is a table that has to be trained?
Check the formula by looking at the wavelength it produces for the first and the last dimension pair.
explanation: The sinusoidal encoding is a fixed function: $\sin$ and $\cos$ of the position divided by $10000^{2k/D}$, giving wavelengths between $2\pi$ and $10000 \cdot 2\pi$. It needs no parameters and can be evaluated at any position, so it extrapolates to longer sequences. A learned encoding costs $N_{max} \times D$ parameters and is limited to $N_{max}$ positions, but performs about equally well in practice.

title: Pretraining the encoder of a dense prediction network
prompt: Which statement about pretraining the encoder of a dense prediction network is correct?

options.text: A classification head consists of global average pooling, a fully connected layer and a softmax.
options.explanation: To pretrain on classification, the feature map is reduced to one vector by global average pooling, mapped to class scores by a fully connected layer and turned into probabilities by a softmax. The head is discarded for the dense task.

options.text: MoCo is a self-distillation method and DINOv2 a contrastive one.
options.explanation: The roles are swapped. MoCo is a contrastive method (queries against a momentum-encoded dictionary of negatives); DINO and DINOv2 are built on self-distillation with a teacher and a student.

options.text: MAE is an example of supervised pretraining with ImageNet labels.
options.explanation: A masked autoencoder is self-supervised: it masks most patches and reconstructs them from the visible ones, without using any labels.

options.text: Only convolutional backbones can be used as encoders.
options.explanation: Any backbone that produces feature maps can be an encoder, including vision transformers (ViT) and hybrids; U-Net-style networks are not tied to convolutions.

hints: Which of these methods use labels, and which create their own training signal?
Contrastive means comparing positive and negative pairs; distillation means matching a teacher.
explanation: Encoders can be pretrained with supervision (a classification head on ImageNet labels) or self-supervision. Contrastive methods such as MoCo pull positive pairs together and push negatives apart; self-distillation methods such as DINOv2 match a student to a teacher; MAE reconstructs masked patches. The encoder is not restricted to CNNs.

title: Output size of the original U-Net
prompt: The original U-Net uses unpadded 3 × 3 convolutions (each one removes 2 pixels from the side length), two per block, four 2 × 2 max pooling steps in the contracting path (each halving the side length) and four 2 × 2 up-convolutions in the expansive path, each doubling the side length. There are two convolutions in each of the five levels of the contracting path (including the bottleneck) and two in each of the four levels of the expansive path. The input tile is 508 × 508. What is the side length of the output segmentation map? Ignore the final 1 × 1 convolution, which does not change the size.
hints: Track the side length level by level: two convolutions subtract 4, a pooling halves, an up-convolution doubles.
The bottleneck also has two convolutions.
explanation:
Contracting path: 508 → conv, conv → 504 → pool → 252 → 248 → pool → 124 → 120 → pool → 60 → 56 → pool → 28 → bottleneck convs → 24.

Expansive path: up-convolution → 48 → convs → 44 → up → 88 → convs → 84 → up → 168 → convs → 164 → up → 328 → convs → 324.

Common wrong results: 328 (forgetting the last two convolutions) or 388 (forgetting the two bottleneck convolutions, which also shifts all later sizes).

title: Bilinear interpolation inside a cell
prompt: Bilinear interpolation is evaluated at the point $P = (x, y) = (1, 3)$ inside the square cell with corners $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(0, 4)$ and $(4, 4)$. The values at the corners are $f(0, 0) = 48$, $f(4, 0) = 80$, $f(0, 4) = 64$ and $f(4, 4) = 112$. What is $f(P)$?
hints: First interpolate along x on the two horizontal edges $y = 0$ and $y = 4$, then interpolate along y between the two results.
The fractional coordinates inside the cell are $x/4$ and $y/4$.
explanation:
The fractional position in the cell is $t_x = 1/4$ and $t_y = 3/4$. Along x at $y = 0$: $48 + 0.25 \cdot (80 - 48) = 56$. Along x at $y = 4$: $64 + 0.25 \cdot (112 - 64) = 76$. Then along y: $56 + 0.75 \cdot (76 - 56) = 71$.

Check with the four weights: $0.1875 \cdot 48 + 0.0625 \cdot 80 + 0.5625 \cdot 64 + 0.1875 \cdot 112 = 9 + 5 + 36 + 21 = 71$.

Common wrong results: swapping the roles of x and y (using $t_x = 3/4$, $t_y = 1/4$) gives 79; averaging the four corners gives 76; taking the nearest corner value $f(0, 4)$ gives 64.

title: Upsampling as cross-attention
prompt: In feature upsampling as cross-attention (JAFAR, LoftUp, AnyUp), queries come from the high-resolution image and keys and values come from the low-resolution feature map. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The output has shape $3 \times H \times W$, like the image the queries come from.
options.explanation: The output are features, not colours: it has the channel dimension $C$ of the low-resolution feature map and the high resolution $H \times W$, i.e. $C \times H \times W$. Only the spatial size is taken over from the image.

options.text: The values are the RGB pixels of the high-resolution image.
options.explanation: The RGB image is only used to compute the queries (and guide the attention). The values are the low-resolution feature vectors that are being upsampled.

options.text: Each output pixel is a softmax-weighted sum of the low-resolution value vectors.
options.explanation: Every high-resolution query is compared with all (or a window of) low-resolution keys, the scores are normalised by a softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the corresponding low-resolution values, like a learned, image-guided interpolation.

options.text: The softmax runs over the queries rather than over the keys.
options.explanation: As in any attention layer the softmax normalises over the keys for each query, so that the weights of one output pixel sum to 1. Normalising over queries would not give a weighted average of values.

hints: What are the values that get averaged: the image or the features you want to upsample?
Which axis must sum to 1 so that each output is a weighted average?
explanation: Cross-attention upsamplers replace fixed interpolation kernels by weights computed from the high-resolution image. For each high-resolution pixel (query), the softmax over the low-resolution keys gives weights that sum to 1, and the output is the weighted average of the low-resolution feature (value) vectors. The output therefore keeps the feature channels of the input and gains the image's resolution.

title: Output size of a transposed convolution
prompt: A transposed convolution, `torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d`, maps 16 input channels to 8 output channels with `kernel_size=4`, `stride=2`, `padding=1` and `output_padding=0` (dilation 1). It receives a 5 × 5 spatial input. What is the output height (equal to the output width)?
hints: Use $H_{out} = (H_{in} - 1) \cdot s - 2p + k + \text{output\_padding}$.
The channel numbers do not influence the spatial size.
explanation:
$$H_{out} = (H_{in} - 1) \cdot s - 2p + k + \text{output\_padding} = (5 - 1) \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 1 + 4 + 0 = 8 - 2 + 4 = 10$$

The kernel 4, stride 2, padding 1 setting is the standard one that exactly doubles the size. Common wrong results: 12 if the padding is ignored ($8 + 4$), 8 if only the stride term is used, or using the ordinary convolution formula $(H + 2p - k)/s + 1$, which gives 2 and is wrong for a transposed convolution. The 16 and 8 channels only affect the parameter count.

title: Hybrid attention and convolution upsampling blocks
prompt: Which statements about hybrid upsampling blocks that combine attention and convolution are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: TransUNet uses a transformer encoder at full resolution and a transformer decoder.
options.explanation: TransUNet applies the transformer to CNN feature maps at a coarse resolution (1/16 of the input), not at full resolution, and its decoder is a convolutional cascaded upsampler, not a transformer.

options.text: In the Mask2Former pixel decoder, the stride-4 feature also passes through the deformable attention layers.
options.explanation: The deformable attention layers process only the coarser multi-scale features (strides 8, 16 and 32). The stride-4 feature is added later through a lateral connection and convolution, which keeps the cost low.

options.text: A DPT fusion block adds the output of the previous, coarser fusion block.
options.explanation: Each DPT fusion block combines the (reassembled) feature of its own scale with the output of the coarser block before it, using residual convolution units and upsampling by a factor of 2, thereby refining the map step by step.

options.text: In deformable attention, each query attends to all pixels of all scales, so the cost is quadratic in the pixel count.
options.explanation: Deformable attention lets each query attend to only a small number of learned sampling points per scale and head, so the cost grows linearly with the number of pixels.

options.text: Each block of TransUNet's cascaded upsampler applies a bilinear ×2 upsampling, a 3 × 3 convolution and a ReLU.
options.explanation: The cascaded upsampler (CUP) of TransUNet stacks blocks that each upsample by 2, apply a 3 × 3 convolution and a ReLU, which gradually recovers the resolution of the token map.

hints: Which parts of these architectures stay convolutional?
What makes deformable attention cheaper than full attention?
explanation: Hybrid decoders combine the global context of attention with the locality of convolution. TransUNet runs a transformer on coarse CNN features and decodes with a convolutional cascaded upsampler; DPT fuses multi-scale features coarse to fine by addition and upsampling; Mask2Former's pixel decoder uses deformable attention, which samples only a few points per query and therefore scales linearly, and leaves the highest-resolution feature to a cheap lateral path.

title: Roles of encoder, decoder and skip connections
prompt: Which statement about the encoder, the decoder and the skip connections of a U-Net is correct?

options.text: The encoder has to be built from the same blocks as in the original paper.
options.explanation: The U-Net idea is the encoder-decoder layout with skips; the encoder can be any backbone (ResNet, ViT, ...) that produces features at several resolutions.

options.text: Skip connections are there to reduce the number of channels in the encoder.
options.explanation: Skips do not change the encoder's channels. They carry high-resolution detail from the encoder to the decoder, where it is concatenated or added to the upsampled features.

options.text: The encoder goes from low to high resolution.
options.explanation: The encoder goes from high to low resolution (downsampling while increasing the channels); the decoder goes from low back to high resolution.

options.text: The decoder mirrors the encoder: each block upsamples and then refines with convolutions.
options.explanation: The decoder reverses the encoder's resolution steps: every block upsamples the feature map, fuses it with the skip feature of the same scale and refines it with convolutions.

hints: In which direction does the resolution change in the encoder?
What information does a skip connection transport?
explanation: A U-Net has an encoder that reduces resolution to gather context, a decoder that mirrors it by upsampling step by step, and skip connections that pass fine spatial detail from encoder to decoder at the matching scale. The encoder blocks can be freely chosen.

title: Aligning skip and decoder feature sizes
prompt: Which statements about aligning the spatial size of the skip feature $x$ and the decoder feature $g$ are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Odd sizes break exact ×2 steps: 75 becomes 37 after pooling and 74 after upsampling.
options.explanation: Pooling with stride 2 floors the size: $\lfloor 75 / 2 \rfloor = 37$, and upsampling by 2 gives 74, which no longer matches the skip's 75.

options.text: With `padding=1` in every 3 × 3 convolution, the sizes match if $H$ and $W$ are divisible by $2^L$ for $L$ pooling steps.
options.explanation: A 3 × 3 convolution with padding 1 keeps the size. If the size is divisible by $2^L$, each pooling halves it exactly and each upsampling doubles it back without rounding errors.

options.text: Cropping the skip drops channels of $x$.
options.explanation: Cropping removes border pixels, i.e. it acts on the spatial dimensions, not on the channels. All channels remain.

options.text: Resizing $g$ by interpolation to the size of $x$ handles any input size.
options.explanation: Interpolating $g$ (e.g. bilinearly) to the spatial size of $x$ produces matching shapes for arbitrary input sizes, at the cost of a small resampling inaccuracy.

options.text: Cropping the skip is the common modern default.
options.explanation: Cropping was needed in the original unpadded U-Net. Modern implementations use padded convolutions (and interpolation or padding when sizes are odd) instead.

hints: What happens to 75 when you halve it with a floor and double it again?
Which dimensions does cropping act on?
explanation: The decoder must produce a feature map of exactly the skip's size before concatenation or addition. This is guaranteed when padded convolutions are used and the input size is divisible by $2^L$; for other sizes one can interpolate the decoder feature to the skip's size (or pad the input). Cropping the skip, as in the original unpadded U-Net, only removes border pixels and is rarely used today.

title: DoubleConv and Up blocks of a PyTorch U-Net
prompt: A PyTorch U-Net uses `DoubleConv(c_in, c_out)` and `Up(c_in, c_out)`, where `Up` applies `ConvTranspose2d(c_in, c_in // 2, kernel_size=2, stride=2)` to `x` and then `DoubleConv(c_in, c_out)` to `torch.cat([skip, x], dim=1)`. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `DoubleConv` is (conv 3 × 3, BatchNorm, ReLU) applied twice.
options.explanation: Two consecutive blocks of 3 × 3 convolution, BatchNorm and ReLU make up a `DoubleConv`, which replaces the two plain convolution-ReLU pairs of the original U-Net.

options.text: After the concatenation, the tensor has `c_in / 2` channels.
options.explanation: The next layer is `DoubleConv(c_in, c_out)`, so the concatenated tensor has `c_in` channels: `c_in // 2` from the up-convolved `x` plus `c_in // 2` from the skip.

options.text: The up-convolution in `Up` halves the channels and doubles the height and the width.
options.explanation: `ConvTranspose2d(c_in, c_in // 2, kernel_size=2, stride=2)` maps `c_in` to `c_in // 2` channels, and $H_{out} = (H - 1) \cdot 2 + 2 = 2H$ (same for the width).

options.text: BatchNorm is a modern addition that the original U-Net did not have.
options.explanation: The original U-Net (2015) used plain convolution plus ReLU without normalisation; BatchNorm is added in most modern implementations because it stabilises and speeds up training.

options.text: The concatenation is along the batch dimension, `dim=0`.
options.explanation: Skip and decoder features are concatenated along the channel dimension, `dim=1` of an $(N, C, H, W)$ tensor. Concatenating along the batch dimension would stack the samples instead of fusing features.

hints: The input of the second `DoubleConv` must have `c_in` channels. Where do they come from?
Which dimension of an $(N, C, H, W)$ tensor is dim=1?
explanation: In `Up`, the transposed convolution halves the channels and doubles the spatial size; concatenation with the skip along the channel dimension (`dim=1`) then restores `c_in` channels, which `DoubleConv(c_in, c_out)` expects. `DoubleConv` itself is two times conv 3 × 3, BatchNorm, ReLU; the BatchNorm is a later addition to the original design.

title: Parametrization of the sampling domain
prompt: Which statements about the parametrization of the sampling domain are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A domain that scales with the number of pixels, such as $[0, 512]$, is typically better for resolution-independent code.
options.explanation: For resolution-independent code a fixed domain such as $[0, 1]$ is preferable, because the same coordinates mean the same physical location at every resolution. A domain such as $[0, 512]$ changes whenever the resolution changes.

options.text: With samples at the cell centers, the outermost samples lie half a pixel inside the domain boundary.
options.explanation: Each sample sits in the middle of its pixel (cell), so the first and last samples are half a cell width away from the domain boundary.

options.text: In PyTorch, `align_corners=False` corresponds to samples at the cell centers and `align_corners=True` to samples at the corners.
options.explanation: With `align_corners=False` the pixels are treated as cells whose centres are the samples; with `align_corners=True` the corner pixels' centres are placed exactly on the domain boundary, so the samples sit at the corners.

options.text: With the domain $[0, 1]^2$ and a $2 \times 2$ grid of center samples, the samples sit at the coordinates 0 and 1.
options.explanation: Two cell-centred samples in $[0, 1]$ lie at the middle of each half, i.e. at 0.25 and 0.75. The coordinates 0 and 1 would be corner samples.

options.text: With samples at the corners, halving the sample spacing turns $n$ samples along one axis into $2n - 1$ samples, not $2n$.
options.explanation: There are $n - 1$ intervals between $n$ corner samples. Halving the spacing doubles the intervals to $2(n - 1)$ and adds one, giving $2n - 1$ samples. With centre samples each cell splits into two cells, giving exactly $2n$.

hints: For $n$ cell-centred samples in $[0, 1]$, the sample positions are $(k + 0.5)/n$.
Count intervals, not samples, when the spacing is halved.
explanation: Two conventions exist for sample positions: cell centers (`align_corners=False`), where the outer samples lie half a cell inside the domain, and corners (`align_corners=True`), where they lie on the boundary. Centre sampling makes a ×2 refinement give exactly $2n$ samples, while corner sampling gives $2n - 1$. A resolution-independent fixed domain such as $[0, 1]$ is preferable to a domain in pixel units.

title: Why attention needs positional encodings
prompt: Explain why a self-attention layer without positional encoding cannot distinguish different orderings of its input vectors, and how adding a positional encoding fixes this. Why is a fixed sinusoidal encoding able to handle longer sequences than a learned one?
model_answer: Self-attention computes each output from the query of that position and the keys and values of all positions with shared weights, so permuting the inputs only permutes the outputs (permutation equivariance); the layer sees a set, not a sequence. Adding a vector that depends on the position to each input breaks this symmetry, since the same content at different positions now gives different queries and keys. A sinusoidal encoding is a closed-form function of the position, so it can be evaluated for positions never seen in training, whereas a learned encoding is a table with entries only up to the maximum training length.
key_points: Shared projection weights and content-only attention make the layer permutation equivariant, so order information is absent.
Adding a position-dependent vector to the inputs makes the same content produce different queries and keys at different positions.
A sinusoidal encoding is a function of the position index and can be computed for any position.
A learned encoding is a lookup table with a fixed maximum length and no values for positions beyond it.
hints: What does the output of attention depend on: the content, the position, or both?
What would you need to do to get the encoding of position 5000 when the training length was 512?
explanation: The model answer rests on the equivariance property: without positional information the order of tokens is invisible to the layer, so any order-dependent task (language, patch arrangement in a ViT) cannot be solved. The usual half-answers say only that positional encodings 'add position information' without explaining that the layer is otherwise permutation equivariant, or claim the sinusoidal encoding is better in accuracy; the real advantage is that it has no parameters and extrapolates to unseen lengths.

source.item: Extra: upsampling artifacts and skip connections

title: Checkerboard artifacts and alternatives
prompt: Explain why a transposed convolution with kernel size 5 and stride 2 produces checkerboard artifacts, and describe two ways to avoid them.
model_answer: In a transposed convolution each input adds a stride-shifted copy of the kernel to the output. With kernel size 5 and stride 2, odd output positions are covered by 2 copies and even positions by 3, so the output is a sum with a regular, uneven pattern that shows up as a checkerboard even if the weights are uniform. It is avoided by choosing a kernel size divisible by the stride (for example 4 with stride 2, where every position gets 2 copies), or by upsampling with interpolation (nearest or bilinear) followed by an ordinary convolution, or by using PixelShuffle after a convolution.
key_points: Each output position receives a different number of kernel copies (3 and 2 alternately) because 5 is not divisible by 2.
The uneven overlap creates a periodic pattern, the checkerboard, in the output.
A kernel size divisible by the stride gives the same number of contributions everywhere.
Interpolation followed by a convolution, or PixelShuffle, are alternatives that avoid uneven overlap.
hints: Count how many shifted copies of the kernel cover each output position.
Which kernel sizes make that count constant?
explanation: The key idea is that the overlap count, not the learned weights, causes the periodic pattern: with kernel size $k$ and stride $s$ it is constant only if $k$ is divisible by $s$. A half-answer that says only 'transposed convolutions create artifacts' misses the cause; another common mistake is to claim that a larger kernel always helps, while kernel 5 with stride 2 is uneven although it is larger than 4.

title: Weights of a convolution after skip concatenation
prompt: A decoder feature $g$ with 256 channels and an aligned skip feature $x$ with 48 channels are fused by concatenation along the channel axis. The result is passed to a 3×3 convolution with 128 output channels (biases ignored). How many weights does this 3×3 convolution have?

parts.label: Number of weights of the 3×3 convolution

hints: Concatenation stacks the channels; it does not add or average them.
The weight count of a convolution is kernel height × kernel width × input channels × output channels.
explanation:
Concatenation along the channel axis gives 256 + 48 = 304 input channels for the convolution. Each of the 128 output channels has a 3×3×304 filter, so the layer has $3\cdot 3\cdot 304\cdot 128 = 2736\cdot 128 = 350{,}208$ weights.

Typical wrong results: counting only the decoder channels gives $9\cdot 256\cdot 128 = 294{,}912$; counting only the skip channels gives $9\cdot 48\cdot 128 = 55{,}296$; treating the layer as a 1×1 convolution gives $304\cdot 128 = 38{,}912$; adding the 128 biases (which the question ignores) gives 350,336. The takeaway: fusing a skip by concatenation widens the next convolution's input, so skips cost parameters.

title: The transposed-convolution up-block
prompt: An up-block takes an input $X$ of shape $C \times H \times W$, applies `ConvTranspose2d(C, C/2, kernel_size=2, stride=2)`, concatenates a skip feature of shape $C/2 \times 2H \times 2W$, and then applies two padded 3×3 conv, BN, ReLU layers. Which statement about this block is correct?

options.text: It is the default up-step in diffusion U-Nets such as Stable Diffusion.
options.explanation: Diffusion U-Nets typically upsample with nearest-neighbour interpolation followed by a convolution (resize-then-convolve), not with a transposed convolution. The transposed-convolution block is the classic choice of the original U-Net.

options.text: A fixed nearest-neighbour upsampling precedes the transposed convolution.
options.explanation: The transposed convolution is itself the upsampling operator: with stride 2 it already doubles H and W. No fixed interpolation is applied before it.

options.text: With kernel 2 and stride 2, neighbouring kernels overlap unevenly, which causes checkerboard artifacts.
options.explanation: With kernel size equal to stride, the kernel footprints tile the output exactly and do not overlap at all, so this setting avoids the uneven overlap. Checkerboard artifacts appear when the kernel size is not divisible by the stride (for example kernel 3, stride 2).

options.text: The two 3×3 conv, BN, ReLU layers refine the result and map C to C/2 channels.
options.explanation: After concatenating the C/2 upsampled channels with the C/2 skip channels there are C channels. The first 3×3 convolution maps C to C/2 and the second keeps C/2, refining the fused features.

hints: Track the channel count: how many channels exist right after the concatenation?
When do the footprints of a transposed convolution overlap?
explanation: The transposed convolution halves the channels (C to C/2) and doubles the resolution; concatenation with the C/2 skip channels brings the count back to C, and the two 3×3 conv blocks then reduce it to C/2 while refining the fused features. Kernel 2 with stride 2 gives non-overlapping footprints, so it is free of the uneven-overlap pattern. Remember the channel bookkeeping: up, concatenate, then reduce with the double convolution.

title: The overlap-tile strategy
prompt: Which statement about the overlap-tile strategy of the original U-Net paper is correct?

options.text: Tiling is needed because otherwise the resolution would be limited by the GPU memory.
options.explanation: Large images do not fit into GPU memory in one forward pass, so they are cut into tiles that are segmented one after another and stitched together seamlessly.

options.text: The whole image is always processed in a single forward pass, whatever its size.
options.explanation: This is exactly what the strategy avoids: big images are split into overlapping tiles precisely because a single pass would exceed the available memory.

options.text: At the image border, the missing context is filled with zeros.
options.explanation: The paper extrapolates the missing context by mirroring the input image at the border, which gives more natural context than a block of zeros.

options.text: The predicted area of a tile is exactly as large as the tile that is fed to the network.
options.explanation: The U-Net uses unpadded (valid) convolutions, so the output segmentation is smaller than the input tile (572×572 in, 388×388 out in the paper). The input tile therefore overlaps its neighbours to supply the context.

hints: Why would a network that loses border pixels in every convolution need overlapping inputs?
explanation: With valid convolutions each tile only yields predictions for its central area, so tiles are fed with extra surrounding context and the predicted areas then tile the image seamlessly. This tiling keeps memory use bounded regardless of image size. At the real image border the context is created by mirroring.

title: Multi-scale outputs and skips from a single-resolution encoder
prompt: Here a tap is the token output of one intermediate ViT layer, and reassembly turns a tap back into an image-like feature map. Which statements about multi-scale outputs and skips from a single-resolution encoder are correct?

options.text: In a feature pyramid, all levels stay as outputs, for example to detect objects of different sizes.
options.explanation: A feature pyramid keeps every scale as a separate output, so that coarse levels can serve large objects and fine levels small ones.

options.text: The extra heads of deep supervision are required at inference.
options.explanation: Deep supervision attaches auxiliary heads only to add loss terms during training and improve gradient flow. At inference they can be discarded and only the final output is used.

options.text: DPT connects its reassembled taps with same-level skips and residual fusion blocks.
options.explanation: DPT reassembles tokens from several ViT layers into feature maps at different scales and merges them with a decoder built from residual fusion blocks, giving skip-like connections to the decoder.

options.text: With multi-scale outputs, every decoder level gets a prediction head: a 1×1 convolution and an upsampling to H×W.
options.explanation: Each decoder level gets a light head that maps its features to class scores (1×1 convolution) and upsamples them to full resolution, so every level can produce or be supervised on a full-size prediction.

options.text: A plain ViT halves its resolution after every few layers, like a CNN encoder.
options.explanation: A plain ViT keeps the same token grid (single resolution) in all layers. There is no downsampling, which is why taps must be reassembled into multiple scales for dense prediction.

hints: Think about which components are only useful for the training loss.
What does the resolution of a plain ViT look like from layer to layer?
explanation: A plain ViT works at one resolution throughout, so multi-scale structure has to be created from taps of different depths (as in DPT) and then used for pyramids or per-level prediction heads. Auxiliary heads of deep supervision exist only to help training and are dropped at test time.

title: Incoming nodes N for the U-Net weight initialisation
prompt: The U-Net paper draws the initial weights from a Gaussian distribution with standard deviation $\sqrt{2/N}$, where $N$ is the number of incoming nodes of one neuron (biases are not counted). Consider a 3×3 convolution that maps the 256 feature channels of the previous layer to 128 feature channels. What is $N$ for this layer?
hints: One output neuron looks at a 3×3 window in every input channel.
The number of output channels does not matter for a single neuron.
explanation:
One output neuron computes a weighted sum over a 3×3 window in each of the 256 input channels, so it has $N = 3\cdot 3\cdot 256 = 2304$ incoming connections. The initial standard deviation is then $\sqrt{2/2304} = \sqrt{1/1152}\approx 0.029$.

Typical wrong results: $3\cdot 3\cdot 128 = 1152$ uses the output channels; $3\cdot 3\cdot 256\cdot 128 = 294{,}912$ is the total weight count of the layer, not the fan-in of one neuron; 256 forgets the 3×3 window; 2305 wrongly counts the bias.

title: Comparing upsampling operators
prompt: Which statements comparing the upsampling operators are correct?

options.text: Among nearest, bilinear, bicubic, bed of nails, pixel shuffle, transposed convolution and convex upsampling, only the last two have learnable parameters.
options.explanation: The first five are fixed rules (interpolation, zero insertion or a pure rearrangement of values). A transposed convolution has a learned kernel and convex upsampling has a learned head that predicts the combination weights.

options.text: A bed of nails keeps one value per r×r block and puts zeros elsewhere.
options.explanation: Bed of nails places each input value at one position of an r×r block of the output and fills the remaining r²−1 positions with zeros.

options.text: A transposed convolution has to keep the channel count unchanged.
options.explanation: A transposed convolution has separate in and out channel counts, like any convolution. The up-block of a U-Net uses it precisely to go from C to C/2 channels.

options.text: Nearest-neighbour interpolation gives a smoother output than bilinear interpolation.
options.explanation: Nearest neighbour just copies values and produces blocky, piecewise-constant output. Bilinear interpolation averages neighbours and is smoother.

options.text: A pixel shuffle maps C·r² × H × W to C × rH × rW by rearranging channels into space.
options.explanation: Pixel shuffle takes each group of r² channels and distributes them over an r×r block of spatial positions. It moves values without any computation, which is why it has no parameters.

hints: Which operators contain a learned kernel or a learned prediction head?
Is pixel shuffle a computation or just a reshuffling of existing numbers?
explanation: Fixed upsamplers (nearest, bilinear, bicubic, bed of nails, pixel shuffle) have no parameters; the learned ones are the transposed convolution and convex upsampling. Pixel shuffle trades channels for resolution, bed of nails inserts zeros, and nearest neighbour is the least smooth of the interpolations.

title: Properties of convex upsampling
prompt: Which statements about convex upsampling as used in RAFT are correct?

options.text: The weights may be negative, which lets the result overshoot at edges.
options.explanation: The weights are made non-negative and sum to 1 (softmax), which is what makes the combination convex. Negative weights would be a general linear filter, as in bicubic interpolation, and could overshoot.

options.text: Convex upsampling works without any learnable parameters.
options.explanation: The combination weights are predicted by a small learned convolutional head from the network features. Only interpolation methods such as bilinear are parameter-free.

options.text: The 9 weights are a fixed kernel that is learned once and used at every pixel.
options.explanation: The 9 weights are predicted separately for every fine pixel from the image content, so they adapt to edges and motion boundaries. A single shared kernel would be an ordinary transposed convolution.

options.text: RAFT upsamples the flow from (H/8) × (W/8) to H × W.
options.explanation: RAFT estimates flow at 1/8 resolution and then upsamples it by a factor of 8 in each dimension to full resolution with convex upsampling.

options.text: A convex combination of 9 values can never lie outside the range of those values.
options.explanation: A convex combination is a weighted average with non-negative weights summing to 1, so it lies between the smallest and largest of the 9 values.

hints: What two conditions define a convex combination of weights?
Are the weights a property of the layer or are they computed from the input?
explanation: Convex upsampling predicts, for every fine pixel, 9 non-negative weights that sum to 1 and applies them to the 3×3 neighbourhood of coarse flow values. Because the result is a weighted average it can never overshoot, and because the weights are content dependent it can place sharp motion boundaries where plain interpolation would blur them.

title: Bottleneck side length of a padded U-Net
prompt: The padded U-Net of the lecture is created as `UNet(c_in=3, n_classes=21, widths=(32, 64, 128, 256))`: a DoubleConv stem, then a 2×2 max pooling followed by a DoubleConv for every further width, mirrored by Up blocks with skip connections, and a 1×1 convolution head. Every 3×3 convolution uses padding=1. The input has shape 2×3×128×128. What is the side length of the bottleneck feature map?

parts.label: Side length of the bottleneck feature map

hints: Padded 3×3 convolutions keep the spatial size; only pooling changes it.
How many widths come after the stem, i.e. how many poolings are there?
explanation:
The stem (width 32) works at 128×128. The remaining three widths (64, 128, 256) are each preceded by a 2×2 max pooling, so the side length goes 128 → 64 → 32 → 16. With padding=1 the 3×3 convolutions do not change the size, so the bottleneck (256 channels) is 16×16 and has shape 2×256×16×16.

Typical wrong results: 8 comes from pooling four times (one per width instead of one per width after the stem); 32 or 64 come from stopping one or two poolings early.

title: Same-level skips versus sparse skips
prompt: Two skip connection patterns are compared: same-level skips, where encoder level $l$ feeds decoder level $l$ (one skip per resolution), and sparse skips, where only one or two levels are connected. Which statement about these patterns is correct?

options.text: DeepLabv3+ uses one skip per resolution, like the plain U-Net.
options.explanation: DeepLabv3+ is the sparse example: it has a single skip that brings one low-level encoder feature to the decoder.

options.text: A limitation of same-level skips is the semantic gap: shallow encoder features meet deep decoder features directly.
options.explanation: Shallow encoder features are low-level (edges, textures) while the decoder features at the same level are already highly semantic. Concatenating them directly mixes very different kinds of information.

options.text: Without skips, boundaries become sharper, because the bottleneck holds all details.
options.explanation: Without skips the decoder must reconstruct fine detail from the low-resolution bottleneck, which has discarded much of it, so boundaries become blurrier. Skips are what bring the high-resolution detail back.

options.text: DeepLabv3+ takes its single skip from stride 32.
options.explanation: Stride 32 is the coarsest, most semantic level and carries little spatial detail. DeepLabv3+ takes its skip from an early, high-resolution layer (stride 4) to recover boundaries.

hints: Which features carry fine spatial detail, early or late ones?
explanation: Same-level skips supply detail at every resolution but force shallow features to meet deep ones, the semantic gap. Sparse skips, as in DeepLabv3+, use only one early (stride 4) feature to restore boundaries. Removing skips altogether hurts boundary sharpness because the bottleneck cannot keep all spatial detail.

title: Structure of the transformer block
prompt: Which statement about the transformer block is correct?

options.text: Vaswani et al. use 12 blocks, $D_{model} = 768$ and 12 heads.
options.explanation: Those numbers describe BERT-base and ViT-Base. The base model of Vaswani et al. uses 6 blocks, $D_{model} = 512$ and 8 heads.

options.text: Layer normalization computes its statistics across all vectors of the set.
options.explanation: Layer normalization normalizes each vector over its own features, independently of the other vectors. That makes it independent of the sequence length and batch, unlike batch normalization.

options.text: The MLP is applied independently to each vector.
options.explanation: The MLP is a position-wise feed-forward network with shared weights applied to every vector separately. Only attention exchanges information between vectors.

options.text: The block has a single residual connection that skips both sub-layers at once.
options.explanation: Each sub-layer (attention and MLP) has its own residual connection, so the block has two.

hints: Which sub-layer is the only one that mixes different vectors?
explanation: A transformer block has two sub-layers, attention and an MLP, each wrapped with its own residual connection and layer normalization. Attention is the only place where vectors interact; the MLP and the layer normalization act on each vector independently.

title: Upsampling blocks, typical use and motivation
prompt: Which statements matching popular upsampling blocks to their typical use and motivation are correct?

options.text: Transformer token decoders reuse conv blocks on the token grid (as in SAM) or attend to any resolution (as in JAFAR).
options.explanation: SAM-style decoders reshape tokens into a grid and reuse convolutional upsampling, while JAFAR uses attention so that features can be upsampled to an arbitrary target resolution.

options.text: Resize-then-convolve is chosen because all of its convolutions run at low resolution.
options.explanation: In resize-then-convolve the image is resized first and the convolution then runs at the higher resolution, which is more expensive. It is chosen to avoid the checkerboard artifacts of transposed convolutions.

options.text: Hybrid attention + conv blocks (DPT, TransUNet, Mask2Former) take global context from attention and detail from conv skips.
options.explanation: Attention gives every location access to global context, while the convolutional skips supply high-resolution local detail. Combining both is the motivation of these hybrid designs.

options.text: Conv-then-pixel-shuffle is the block chosen for diffusion U-Nets, because it has no checkerboard artifacts.
options.explanation: Diffusion U-Nets typically use nearest upsampling followed by a convolution. Conv-then-pixel-shuffle is the typical block of super-resolution networks, and its motivation is cheap upsampling with the convolutions at low resolution.

options.text: The transposed conv block is the standard choice in super-resolution networks such as ESPCN and EDSR.
options.explanation: ESPCN and EDSR use a convolution followed by pixel shuffle. The transposed convolution block is the classic choice for U-Net decoders.

hints: Match each block to the family of models that made it popular.
Where does the convolution run in each block: before or after the resolution increase?
explanation: Each upsampling block has a typical home: transposed convolutions in classic U-Net decoders, resize-then-convolve in diffusion U-Nets (avoiding checkerboard artifacts), conv-then-pixel-shuffle in super-resolution (cheap, low-resolution convolutions) and attention or hybrid blocks in transformer-based models. Be careful with the motivation as well: the cost of a convolution depends on whether it runs before or after the resolution increase.

title: The matrix view of transposed convolution
prompt: Which statement about the matrix view that gives the transposed convolution its name is correct?

options.text: For a 3×3 kernel and a 4×4 tensor (no padding, stride 1), the transposed matrix has shape 16×4 and maps a 2×2 input to a 4×4 output.
options.explanation: The 3×3 kernel on a 4×4 input gives a 2×2 output, so the convolution matrix has shape 4×16 (4 outputs, 16 inputs). Its transpose has shape 16×4 and maps the 4 values of a flattened 2×2 input to 16 values, i.e. a 4×4 output.

options.text: Applying a convolution and then the matching transposed convolution returns the original input values exactly.
options.explanation: The transposed convolution only restores the shape, not the values. The product $C^\top C$ is generally not the identity, so the original input is not recovered.

options.text: The convolution matrix is dense: none of its entries are zero.
options.explanation: Each output row only touches the 9 input positions under the kernel, so in the 4×16 matrix at most 9 of 16 entries per row are non-zero (the matrix is sparse and banded).

options.text: The name comes from transposing the input tensor before an ordinary convolution.
options.explanation: The name refers to transposing the convolution matrix $C$ that expresses the convolution as a matrix-vector product, not to transposing the input tensor.

hints: Write the convolution as a matrix-vector product on the flattened input. What shape must the matrix have?
Does multiplying by $C^\top$ undo multiplying by $C$?
explanation: A convolution can be written as $y = Cx$ with the flattened input $x$. For a 3×3 kernel on a 4×4 input, $x$ has 16 entries and $y$ has 4, so $C$ is 4×16 and sparse. The transposed convolution multiplies by $C^\top$ (16×4), which maps 4 values to 16 and so upsamples from 2×2 to 4×4, but it is not an inverse: only the shapes match.

title: Gating a skip connection
prompt: Which statement about gating a skip connection is correct?

options.text: A gate lets the encoder decide which decoder features pass.
options.explanation: The direction is reversed: the gating signal comes from the decoder and decides which encoder skip features are passed on.

options.text: Gating a skip adds no parameters.
options.explanation: The gate contains learned layers (the 1×1 convolutions that process the skip feature and the gating signal, plus the final 1×1 convolution), so it adds parameters.

options.text: The gated skip is $\alpha$ added to $x$.
options.explanation: The gate computes a map $\alpha \in [0,1]$ and multiplies the skip feature by it, $\alpha \odot x$. Adding it would not suppress anything.

options.text: In the additive attention gate, the sum goes through a ReLU, a 1×1 convolution to one channel and a sigmoid.
options.explanation: The projected skip and gating features are added, passed through a ReLU, reduced by a 1×1 convolution to one channel and squashed by a sigmoid, giving one attention coefficient in [0, 1] per position.

hints: Is the attention coefficient used additively or multiplicatively?
Which of the two inputs is the gating signal?
explanation: In an additive attention gate the decoder's gating signal and the skip feature are projected and summed, then pass ReLU, a 1×1 convolution to one channel and a sigmoid to give a spatial map $\alpha$ in [0, 1]. The skip feature is multiplied by $\alpha$, so irrelevant encoder positions are suppressed before they reach the decoder. The gate is learned and therefore adds parameters.

title: Properties of the attention weight matrix
prompt: In the attention layer, $A = \text{softmax}(E, \text{dim}=1)$ has shape $N_Q \times N_X$: one row per query and one column per input vector. Which statements are correct?

options.text: For a given query, the input vector whose key has the largest similarity receives the largest weight.
options.explanation: Softmax is monotonic, so within a row the largest similarity gives the largest weight.

options.text: An attention weight is negative when the corresponding similarity is negative.
options.explanation: Softmax outputs $e^{e_{ij}}/\sum_k e^{e_{ik}}$, which is always strictly positive, even for a negative similarity. A negative similarity just yields a small weight.

options.text: Each output vector is a convex combination of the value vectors.
options.explanation: Each row of $A$ is non-negative and sums to 1, and the output is $AV$, so every output is a weighted average of the value vectors.

options.text: A query whose similarities are all negative has attention weights that sum to less than 1.
options.explanation: Softmax normalizes the row, so the weights sum to exactly 1 whatever the signs of the similarities.

options.text: The attention weights of one input vector sum to 1 over the queries.
options.explanation: The softmax runs over dim=1, i.e. along each row, over the input vectors. The columns (one input vector across all queries) have no normalization and can sum to anything.

hints: Over which axis does the softmax normalize?
What are the two properties of every row of a softmax output?
explanation: Softmax over dim=1 turns each row of the similarity matrix into a probability distribution over the input vectors: all entries are positive and the row sums to 1. Consequently every output $Y = AV$ is a convex combination of the values, with the largest weight on the best-matching key. Normalization is per query (row), not per input vector (column).

title: The encoder-decoder transformer of Vaswani et al.
prompt: Which statements about the encoder-decoder transformer of Vaswani et al. are correct?

options.text: Both the encoder block and the decoder block are repeated N times.
options.explanation: The encoder is a stack of N identical encoder blocks and the decoder a stack of N identical decoder blocks (N = 6 in the original paper).

options.text: A decoder block contains three sub-layers: masked multi-head self-attention, multi-head cross-attention and a feed-forward sub-layer.
options.explanation: The decoder block first applies masked self-attention to its own sequence, then cross-attention to the encoder output, then a feed-forward network.

options.text: The output probabilities are produced directly by the encoder.
options.explanation: The probabilities come from the decoder: its output goes through a final linear layer and a softmax over the vocabulary. The encoder only produces a representation of the input sequence.

options.text: The encoder uses masked self-attention so that it cannot look ahead.
options.explanation: The encoder uses unmasked self-attention: all input positions may attend to each other. The causal mask is needed only in the decoder, which generates the output step by step.

options.text: The decoder is fed the output sequence shifted right.
options.explanation: During training the decoder input is the target sequence shifted right by one position, so the prediction at position $i$ is made only from earlier tokens.

hints: Where is it important that a position cannot see the future?
explanation: The encoder (N blocks of self-attention and feed-forward) builds a representation of the full input; the decoder (N blocks of masked self-attention, cross-attention and feed-forward) predicts the output one token at a time from the shifted-right target and the encoder output, followed by a linear layer and softmax. Masking is a decoder-only mechanism because only the decoder generates sequentially.

title: Intersection over union of one class
prompt: For one class, the predicted mask $A$ contains 80 pixels, the ground-truth mask $B$ contains 80 pixels, and 60 pixels belong to both masks. What is the IoU of this class? Give the answer with two decimals.
hints: The union is not the sum of the two sizes: the overlap is counted twice in that sum.
IoU = intersection / union.
explanation:
The intersection is $|A\cap B| = 60$. The union is $|A\cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A\cap B| = 80 + 80 - 60 = 100$. Hence $\text{IoU} = 60/100 = 0.60$.

Typical wrong results: dividing by the sum $80 + 80 = 160$ without removing the overlap gives 0.375; $60/80 = 0.75$ divides by one mask only (that is precision or recall, and it also equals the Dice coefficient $2\cdot 60/160 = 0.75$ here).

title: Output channels of a convex-upsampling weight head
prompt: Convex upsampling in the style of RAFT upsamples a 2-channel flow field by a factor of 4 in each spatial dimension, from 24×24 to 96×96. Each fine pixel is a convex combination of the 3×3 grid of its nearest coarse neighbours. How many output channels does the weight-prediction head have?

parts.label: Output channels of the weight head

hints: Each coarse pixel must provide weights for all the fine pixels it covers.
Each fine pixel needs one weight per coarse neighbour.
explanation:
Each coarse pixel covers a 4×4 block of fine pixels, i.e. 16 sub-positions. Each fine pixel needs 9 weights (one per 3×3 coarse neighbour), so the head outputs $4\cdot 4\cdot 9 = 144$ channels at 24×24 resolution. The same weights are applied to both flow channels, so the number of flow channels does not matter.

Typical wrong results: 288 multiplies by the 2 flow channels; 576 is the value for RAFT's factor 8 ($8\cdot 8\cdot 9$); 16 or 9 forget one of the two factors.

title: Cross-attention versus self-attention
prompt: Which statement comparing cross-attention and self-attention is correct?

options.text: In image captioning with attention, the queries are CNN features and the keys are decoder states.
options.explanation: It is the other way round: the queries come from the decoder (the words generated so far) and the keys and values come from the CNN features of the image.

options.text: Self-attention has no query matrix, because the inputs are used as queries without any projection.
options.explanation: Self-attention also projects the inputs with learned matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$. The only difference is that all three projections are applied to the same sequence.

options.text: Cross-attention produces one output vector per query.
options.explanation: The output is $AV$ with $A$ of shape $N_Q \times N_X$, so there is one output vector for each query, however many input vectors there are.

options.text: Self-attention needs a second sequence that supplies the queries.
options.explanation: Self-attention computes queries, keys and values from the same sequence. A second sequence supplying the queries is what defines cross-attention.

hints: Which sequence provides the queries in cross-attention, and what determines the number of outputs?
explanation: In both variants queries, keys and values are linear projections of some input; self-attention takes all three from one sequence, cross-attention takes the queries from one sequence and the keys and values from another. The number of outputs always equals the number of queries, so in captioning the decoder states ask questions about the image features.

title: How modern transformers differ from the original
prompt: Which statement about how modern transformers differ from the original design is correct?

options.text: Rotary embeddings are added to the input vectors before the first layer.
options.explanation: Rotary embeddings rotate the queries and keys inside every attention layer, so the attention scores depend on relative positions. Adding position information to the input is the older absolute positional encoding.

options.text: In a mixture of experts, every token is processed by all MLPs and the results are averaged.
options.explanation: A router sends each token to only a few (top-k) experts, which keeps the compute per token small even though the total parameter count is large.

options.text: RMSNorm adds a second shift parameter on top of layer normalization.
options.explanation: RMSNorm is a simplification: it rescales by the root mean square and drops the mean subtraction and the shift parameter. It is cheaper than layer normalization.

options.text: With SwiGLU, the hidden width of the MLP is about $\frac{8}{3}D$.
options.explanation: SwiGLU uses three weight matrices instead of two. To keep the parameter count of the usual MLP with hidden width $4D$ ($2\cdot 4D\cdot D = 8D^2$), the hidden width is reduced to $\frac{8}{3}D$, since $3\cdot\frac{8}{3}D\cdot D = 8D^2$.

hints: Count the weight matrices of a gated MLP and compare to the standard one.
Where in the network does a rotary embedding act?
explanation: Modern transformers change several parts: rotary embeddings act on queries and keys, RMSNorm drops the mean and the shift, mixture of experts activates only a few MLPs per token, and gated MLPs such as SwiGLU shrink the hidden width to about $\frac{8}{3}D$ so that the three-matrix MLP has the same parameter count as the two-matrix MLP with width $4D$.

title: Properties of transposed convolution
prompt: Which statements about transposed convolution are correct?

options.text: It reduces the spatial resolution.
options.explanation: With stride greater than 1 a transposed convolution increases the spatial resolution; reducing it is the job of a strided convolution or pooling.

options.text: Where filter copies overlap in the output, they are summed.
options.explanation: Each input pixel scales a copy of the filter that is placed in the output. Where copies overlap their values are added, which is the transpose of the sliding-window product.

options.text: There is one filter placement per input pixel.
options.explanation: Every input pixel multiplies the filter and writes the scaled copy at its own (strided) location, so the number of placements equals the number of input pixels.

options.text: It computes the exact inverse of a convolution, which is why it is also called deconvolution.
options.explanation: It only reverses the shape change, not the values: it is the transpose of the convolution matrix, not its inverse. The name deconvolution is misleading.

options.text: In 1D, a filter of size 3 with stride 2 and no padding gives exactly twice the input length once one output value is cropped.
options.explanation: For an input of length $n$ the output length is $(n-1)\cdot 2 + 3 = 2n + 1$. Cropping one value gives exactly $2n$.

hints: Think of the operation as stamping a scaled copy of the filter for every input pixel.
For the 1D case, compute the output length with $(n-1)s + k$.
explanation: A transposed convolution places one scaled filter copy per input pixel at stride-spaced positions and sums the overlaps, so the output grows to $(n-1)s + k$ in 1D. With $k=3$, $s=2$ this is $2n+1$, which becomes $2n$ after cropping one value. It is the transpose of the convolution matrix and not its inverse, so values are not recovered.

title: Checkerboard artifacts of transposed convolution
prompt: Explain why a transposed convolution with kernel size 3 and stride 2 can produce checkerboard artifacts, why kernel size 2 with stride 2 does not, and how resize-then-convolve avoids the problem.
model_answer: A transposed convolution stamps a scaled copy of the kernel for every input pixel and sums the overlaps. With kernel 3 and stride 2 the copies overlap in some output positions (two contributions) but not in others (one contribution), so the output receives an uneven, periodic amount of kernel mass and a regular grid pattern appears. With kernel 2 and stride 2 the copies tile the output exactly with no overlap, so every output pixel gets exactly one contribution. Resize-then-convolve first upsamples with a fixed interpolation (for example nearest neighbour) and then applies an ordinary convolution, whose uniform sliding window gives every output pixel the same number of contributions.
key_points: Transposed convolution places one kernel copy per input pixel and sums overlaps.
If the kernel size is not divisible by the stride, overlaps are uneven and periodic, producing the checkerboard.
Kernel size equal to stride gives no overlap, hence uniform coverage.
Resize-then-convolve separates upsampling (fixed interpolation) from feature extraction (a uniformly sliding convolution).
hints: Count how many kernel copies contribute to each output position.
What happens to the coverage when kernel size equals stride?
explanation: The artifact is a coverage problem, not a learning problem: it comes from how many kernel copies add up at each output position. A good answer connects the overlap count to the relation between kernel size and stride and names the fix. Common half-answers: saying the artifacts come from the learned weights, or claiming that every stride-2 transposed convolution shows them (kernel 2 does not), or forgetting that resize-then-convolve costs more because the convolution runs at the higher resolution.

title: Why attention outputs are weighted averages
prompt: Explain how the attention weights are computed from queries and keys, which properties they have, and what this implies for the output vectors. Why is the MLP in a transformer block still needed even though attention already mixes the values?
model_answer: The similarities between queries and keys form a matrix $E$, and a softmax along the input axis turns each row into positive weights that sum to 1. Each output vector is then the weighted average of the value vectors, i.e. a convex combination that cannot leave the range of the values. Attention is the only operation that mixes information between vectors, but it only forms weighted averages of (linear projections of) the inputs. The MLP adds a non-linear transformation applied independently to each vector, increasing the expressive power of the block.
key_points: Weights come from query-key similarities followed by a softmax over the input vectors (per query).
Each row is positive and sums to 1, so every output is a convex combination of the values.
Attention mixes information across vectors, but only through weighted averages of linear projections.
The MLP supplies the per-vector non-linearity and extra capacity.
hints: Over which axis is the softmax taken, and what does that make true for every row?
What kind of function is a weighted average of linear projections?
explanation: The key facts are the row-wise softmax (positive weights summing to 1) and the resulting convex combination of values. The second half tests understanding of the division of labour in a block: attention routes information between vectors, the MLP processes each vector non-linearly.
