Common mistakes: normalizing over queries instead of over inputs, saying weights can be negative, or claiming that attention alone is non-linear in the values (it is linear in the values for fixed weights).

title: Parameters of one transformer block

parts.label: Total parameters of the listed parts

hints: Handle the three groups separately: attention, MLP, layer norms.
Does the number of heads change the size of the $D \times D$ projection matrices?
explanation:
Attention: four matrices of $128 \cdot 128 = 16{,}384$ each, so $4 \cdot 16{,}384 = 65{,}536$. The 8 heads do not change this: each head uses a slice of width $D/8 = 16$ of the same $D \times D$ matrices.

MLP: $W_1$ has $128 \cdot 512 = 65{,}536$ entries and $W_2$ has the same number, so $131{,}072$.

Layer norms: each has $\gamma$ and $\beta$ of length 128, i.e. $256$, so two of them hold $512$.

Total: $65{,}536 + 131{,}072 + 512 = 197{,}120$.

Typical wrong results: also counting the MLP biases ($512 + 128 = 640$) gives $197{,}760$; forgetting the layer norms gives $196{,}608$; multiplying the attention matrices by the 8 heads over-counts them, because the heads split $D$ rather than replicate it.

title: Entry of a 1D transposed convolution
prompt: A 1D transposed convolution with stride 2 and no padding is applied to the input $[5, 1, 3]$ with the filter $[3, 1, 2]$. Nothing is cropped from the output, and output entries are numbered from 1. What is output entry 5?
hints: Each input value stamps a copy of the filter, scaled by that value, into the output; consecutive stamps are shifted by the stride.
The output has length $(3-1)\cdot 2 + 3 = 7$. Which stamps overlap at entry 5?

title: Bicubic interpolation and aliasing
prompt: Which statements about bicubic interpolation and aliasing are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Bicubic interpolation uses a 2 × 2 neighbourhood, like bilinear interpolation.
options.explanation: Bilinear interpolation uses the 2 × 2 nearest pixels, but bicubic uses a 4 × 4 neighbourhood (16 pixels), which is what lets it fit a smooth cubic surface.

options.text: Aliasing is avoided by low-pass filtering after downsampling.
options.explanation: After downsampling the high frequencies have already folded onto low ones and cannot be separated again. The low-pass filter has to be applied before subsampling.

options.text: A low-pass filter is needed before upsampling, but not before downsampling.
options.explanation: This reverses the rule. Downsampling shrinks the sampling rate, so frequencies above the new Nyquist limit must be removed first; upsampling does not need that pre-filter.

options.text: Upsampling does not cause aliasing, because the finer grid can represent every frequency of the input.
options.explanation: The new grid has a higher Nyquist limit than the old one, so every frequency present in the input is representable. Upsampling can blur or create imaging artifacts, but it does not fold frequencies.

options.text: The negative lobes of the bicubic kernel can overshoot at edges, which is called ringing.
options.explanation: The bicubic kernel has negative side lobes, so near a sharp edge the interpolated values can exceed the neighbouring pixel values, producing halos known as ringing.

hints: Think about what the Nyquist limit of the old and new grid is in each direction of resampling.
How many pixels does bicubic interpolation look at per output value?
explanation: Aliasing happens when a signal is sampled at too low a rate: frequencies above half the sampling rate fold onto lower ones. Therefore downsampling needs a low-pass filter before subsampling, while upsampling moves to a finer grid and cannot alias. Bicubic interpolation uses a 4 × 4 neighbourhood and a kernel with negative lobes, which gives sharper results than bilinear but can overshoot (ringing) at edges.

title: Bilinear x2 upsampling as a transposed convolution
prompt: Which statement about writing bilinear x2 upsampling as a transposed convolution is correct?

options.text: It mixes all channels, which corresponds to groups = 1.
options.explanation: Interpolation is done on each channel independently and never mixes channels, so the transposed convolution must be depthwise (groups equal to the number of channels), with the same kernel for each channel.

options.text: The equivalence with F.interpolate holds only at the border pixels.
options.explanation: It is the other way round: the equivalence holds for the interior pixels, where the kernel overlaps fully. At the border the two differ because F.interpolate replicates the edge value while the transposed convolution implicitly zero-pads.

options.text: FCN initializes its transposed convolutions with random weights.
options.explanation: FCN initializes its upsampling layers with bilinear-interpolation weights, so training starts from a sensible upsampler, and the weights can then be learned further.

options.text: The 4 × 4 kernel is the outer product of [0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25] with itself.
options.explanation: For x2 upsampling the 1D bilinear kernel (stride 2, width 4) is [0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25]. The 2D kernel is separable, so it equals the outer product of this vector with itself.

hints: Should interpolation of an RGB image mix the red, green and blue channels?
With stride 2, each output pixel is a weighted combination of its two nearest input pixels in each direction. What are those weights?
explanation: Bilinear interpolation is separable and acts per channel, so as a transposed convolution it is a depthwise layer (groups = channels) with a 4 × 4 kernel that is the outer product of the 1D kernel [0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25]. With stride 2 and padding 1 this reproduces F.interpolate on interior pixels, and edge handling differs at the border. FCN uses exactly this kernel as the initialization of its learnable upsampling layers, rather than random values.

title: Output of a masked attention position with equal scores
prompt: A masked (causal) self-attention layer processes 5 input vectors in sequence order, so position $i$ may only attend to positions $j \le i$. The value vectors are scalars ($D_V = 1$): $V_1 = 7$, $V_2 = 3$, $V_3 = 3$, $V_4 = 7$, $V_5 = 9$. Assume that all similarities $E_{i,j}$ that are not masked are equal. What is the output $Y_4$ of position 4?
hints: Which positions is position 4 allowed to look at?
If all unmasked scores are equal, what are the softmax weights over those positions?
explanation:
Position 4 may attend to positions 1-4; position 5 is masked and receives weight 0. The four unmasked scores are equal, so the softmax gives each weight $1/4$. Then

$$Y_4 = \tfrac{1}{4}(7 + 3 + 3 + 7) = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5.$$

Typical wrong results: including the masked future value $V_5$ and averaging over all five positions gives $29/5 = 5.8$; taking only the current value gives 7; averaging only the previous positions (1-3) gives $13/3 \approx 4.33$. With equal scores, masked attention returns the running mean of the visible values.

title: Shapes and roles in a U-Net upsampling block
prompt: An upsampling block in a decoder chains up to four steps: upsample, project, fuse (with a skip feature) and refine. The block sits in a U-Net whose channel count doubles at every encoder level and receives an input $X$ of shape $C \times H \times W$. Which statement about this block is correct?

options.text: The upsample step has to be a learnable operator.
options.explanation: Upsampling can be a fixed operator such as nearest-neighbour or bilinear interpolation. A learnable transposed convolution is one option, not a requirement.

options.text: The project step changes the spatial size.
options.explanation: The project step is typically a 1 × 1 convolution that changes the number of channels (for example from $C$ to $C/2$) but leaves $H$ and $W$ unchanged. The spatial size is changed by the upsample step.

options.text: The fuse step is mandatory in every upsampling block.
options.explanation: The block chains up to four steps, and fusing with a skip feature is only done when a skip connection exists. Decoders without skip connections just upsample, project and refine.

options.text: The skip feature that is fused has shape C/2 × 2H × 2W.
options.explanation: The upsample step doubles the spatial size to $2H \times 2W$. The encoder level at that resolution has half as many channels as the current one, because channels double at every encoder level, so its skip feature is $C/2 \times 2H \times 2W$.

hints: Which of the four steps changes the spatial size and which changes the number of channels?
Going one level up in the encoder, how do the spatial size and the channel count change?
explanation: In a U-Net, each decoder step undoes one encoder level: the spatial size doubles and, since the encoder doubled the channels on the way down, the channel count halves. The upsample step produces the larger map (by any method, learned or not), the project step adapts the channels, and the optional fuse step concatenates or adds the skip feature from the encoder level of the same resolution, which therefore has shape $C/2 \times 2H \times 2W$.

title: Why downsampling needs a low-pass filter but upsampling does not
prompt: Explain why an image should be low-pass filtered before it is downsampled, whereas upsampling does not need such a filter. What kind of artifact can interpolation kernels with negative lobes (such as bicubic) introduce instead?
model_answer: Downsampling lowers the sampling rate and with it the Nyquist limit, so frequencies above the new limit cannot be represented and fold onto lower frequencies (aliasing). Once folded they cannot be removed, so the image must be low-pass filtered before subsampling. Upsampling moves to a finer grid whose Nyquist limit is higher, so every input frequency is representable and nothing folds. Kernels with negative lobes, such as bicubic, can overshoot next to sharp edges, which appears as ringing.
key_points: Downsampling lowers the Nyquist limit, so frequencies above it fold onto lower ones (aliasing).
The filter must come before subsampling because aliased frequencies cannot be separated afterwards.
Upsampling uses a finer grid that can represent all input frequencies, so it does not alias.
Negative kernel lobes (bicubic) can overshoot at edges, causing ringing.
hints: What happens to a high-frequency pattern when you keep only every second pixel?
Compare the Nyquist limit of the old and the new grid in both directions.
explanation: The model answer rests on the Nyquist limit: the highest frequency a grid can represent is half its sampling rate. When subsampling, content above the new limit is not lost but misrepresented as lower-frequency content, so the filter has to act before. Common half-answers: saying the filter can be applied afterwards (too late), or saying upsampling needs a low-pass filter to avoid aliasing (it does not alias, although it may blur). Ringing is the price paid by sharper kernels like bicubic.

title: What the causal mask does to attention
prompt: Explain how the causal mask in self-attention is applied to the similarity scores and why it is necessary when a model is trained to predict the next element of a sequence. What does the output of a position look like if all its unmasked scores are equal?
model_answer: The mask sets the scores of future positions $j > i$ to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so they get weight exactly 0 and each position is a weighted average of the values at positions up to itself only. This is needed in next-element prediction because otherwise position $i$ could read the very element it is supposed to predict, and training would be trivial. If all unmasked scores are equal, the softmax is uniform over the visible positions, so the output is the plain mean of the values $V_1, \dots, V_i$.
key_points: Scores of future positions are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, giving them weight 0.
Without the mask a position could look at the target it must predict, so training would leak the answer.
Each position's output is a convex combination of values at positions up to itself.
Equal unmasked scores give uniform weights, i.e. the mean of the visible values.
hints: At which point of the computation is the mask applied: before or after the softmax?
Which positions does the softmax normalise over after masking?
explanation: Masking before the softmax matters because the weights of the remaining positions must still sum to 1, which happens automatically when the masked scores are $-\infty$ and so contribute $\exp(-\infty) = 0$. Setting weights to zero after the softmax would leave weights that do not sum to 1. A frequent half-answer is to say the mask only saves computation; its real role is to prevent information leaking from the future during training and to make training match generation, where the future does not exist yet.
